scenario: An unseen item at the bottom of a page is not necessarily disliked, and a once-preferred answer may not stay preferred. ICE incorporates browsing depth into page evaluation, while PEARL restores exploration using new feedback. FocalSwap holds targets and candidates fixed while changing historical search behaviour: conclusions about a signal’s value also depend on what replaces it.

papers.title: Data-Efficient Scaling-Law Discovery for Recommendation Systems via Coupled Hyperparameter Scaling
papers.authors: John Martabano Landy, Louis C. Tiao, Yao Xuan, Luc Kien Hang, Rupinder P. Khandpur, Arvind M. Vepa, Srinidhi Raghavendran, Anirudh Agrawal, Xiaoyi Leo Liu, Jiang Liu, Peggy Yao, Alireza Vahdatpour, Djordje Gligorijevic
papers.abstract: Large-scale ranking and recommendation models of Web platforms benefit from increased compute much as large language models do, and their scaling behavior is broadly power-law in form. Yet ranking models have heterogeneous architectures which makes their scaling law less straightforward than that of LLMs. We address how to discover the scaling law of an arbitrary ranking model efficiently. We introduce a scaling layer, which groups primitive architecture parameters into semantically coherent groups and defines how they co-vary, inducing a mapping from a low-dimensional space of hyper-hyperparameters into the full architecture space. On top of it, Axia fits scaling-informed surrogates, selects configurations by a posterior-based acquisition criterion, and returns a Pareto frontier from which per-model operating points are validated -- replacing exhaustive sweeps with a small number of informative runs. A fleet-level evaluation protocol, computed on a fixed representative model set under matched trial budgets, makes refinements to either component measurable. Our contribution is an automated system that learns model-specific complexity-quality relationships and gives uncertainty-aware guidance for allocating compute across a heterogeneous model ecosystem. Across 34 model iterations in two development cycles on Meta's ads ranking and retrieval system, the workflow yielded a mean 0.66% offline normalized-entropy improvement and 0.36% cumulative online lift.
papers.summary: Expanding a recommender changes interacting embedding dimensions, interaction depth and width; sweeping them separately quickly exhausts training budgets. Meta’s Axia ties the hidden widths of multiple interaction modules together, controlling embedding dimension and interaction depth separately. It profiles inference FLOPs, selects configurations using probabilistic quality and cost predictions, and updates predictions after training. Both adaptive and random search receive 20 full training runs in the main comparison of observed quality–cost frontiers. Across two deployment cycles and 34 model iterations, normalised cross-entropy improved by an average 0.66%, an observational comparison with prior deployments. A small set of experiments can provide evidence for scaling decisions.

papers.title: From Waste to Discovery: Recycling High-Scored Unexposed Candidates in Taobao Feed Recommendation
papers.authors: Ge Fan, Kai Meng, Huiping Chu, Yuning Jiang, Han Zhu, Bo Zheng
papers.abstract: Helping users discover new interests is vital to the long-term health of industrial recommender systems, yet the usual remedy, boosting exposure of under-explored (discovery) content, often backfires in production. We report URED (Unexposed Recycling for Efficient Discovery), a training-free recall-stage system serving Taobao feed recommendation at Alibaba for over six months to tens of millions of daily active users. It rests on a production-validated insight: naive boosting fails because it injects cold, information-poor candidates that rankers systematically over-estimate, buying no discovery gain while risking engagement. Items scored highly but never exposed (signals industrial pipelines routinely discard) form a pool that is both relevant and reliably predictable. Over a 30-day horizon URED aggregates them and re-injects at recall time through a lightweight pipeline spanning offline storage, distributed aggregation, and low-latency online serving, adding under 1% latency via a single O(1) lookup per request with no model retraining. Online A/B tests show +3.47% discovered categories and +8.47% content richness with engagement preserved: completion video views rise significantly (+2.62%) and total views move positive (+0.36%, not significant). Ablations confirm both design pillars are necessary: a one-day window collapses the discovery gain to +0.55% (not significant), and random injection without score filtering yields no gain while trending negative on engagement (-0.17%). Across production recall channels, URED reaches 13.9x the platform-average discovery rate (6.3x the strongest nearline baseline) at engagement quality on par with the platform average. We share deployment details and lessons for practitioners facing the exploration-exploitation dilemma under tight resource constraints.
papers.summary: Ranking already scores many candidates that never reach the screen. This work reuses the high-scoring part of those results to help users encounter additional categories. It accumulates these candidates per user over a month, keeps categories absent from recent exposure, and adds the results to recall. In Taobao feed experiments, new categories actually exposed to users increased by 3.47% and completion video views by 2.62%, both statistically significant. Total video views did not change significantly. The intervention changes how candidates are retained and reused; it requires no ranker retraining.

papers.title: Beyond Independent Predictions: Learning the Browsing Journey for Sequence-Level Re-ranking
papers.authors: Jiayi Zhang, Jingxin Hai, Zhenjia Ma, Hongbin Pei, Dagui Chen, Han Zhu, Jian Xu
papers.abstract: Re-ranking aims to present users with an ordered list that maximizes sequence-level utility. Industrial deployments widely adopt the Generator--Evaluator framework, where the generator proposes candidate sequences, and the evaluator scores them to select the best one for display. The fidelity of the evaluator's utility estimates thus directly governs recommendation quality. However, existing evaluators predominantly follow the \textbf{Independent Behavior Modeling (IBM)} paradigm, which simplifies the continuous user \emph{browsing journey} into independent per-item predictions (e.g., CTR). This oversimplification ignores two physical realities: (i) a click can occur only after the item has been reached and impressed, and (ii) items compete for finite user attention. As a result, IBM produces systematically biased evaluations and suboptimal sequence selection. To address this, we propose a \textbf{Joint Behavior Modeling (JBM)} perspective that explicitly models the \emph{display} $\rightarrow$ \emph{impression} $\rightarrow$ \emph{click} process to capture causal and competitive dependencies within a sequence. Building on JBM, we develop the \textbf{Impression-Click Evaluator (ICE)}, a plug-and-play framework that (i) predicts a browsing-depth distribution to estimate per-position impression probabilities, (ii) leverages predicted impressions to suppress spurious context from unexposed items during click modeling, and (iii) introduces a click distribution matching objective to capture intra-sequence dependencies. Extensive offline experiments across diverse backbones, together with a 14-day online A/B test in the Taobao App (+0.70\% clicks, +3.67\% revenue) and full-traffic deployment, validate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.
papers.summary: A displayed page does not guarantee that users reach its tail; adding item CTRs can overestimate the page’s value. ICE, a whole-page re-ranking evaluator, predicts browsing depth, multiplies each position’s impression probability by its conditional click probability and scores candidate pages. A two-week Taobao experiment kept the sequence generator unchanged; the complete framework increased clicks by 0.70% and commercial revenue by 3.67%. The intervention changes how a page is evaluated, rather than generating more possible orders.

papers.title: Do Search-Augmented Recommenders Use the Latest Search Episode?
papers.abstract: Search-augmented recommenders can use the latest search episode and earlier searches. We introduce FocalSwap to test how these inputs contribute to the next recommendation. For each recommendation, it changes the latest search slot or all search inputs while holding the target, candidates, pre-search history, and scorer fixed. It compares neutral masks with matched observed-search replacements, recording rank changes, RR gains relative to each control, and preference for the true focal search. A planted signal and GenSAR's current-query task confirm that the audit detects known input dependence. We evaluate behavioral and lexical evidence on KuaiSAR and Qilin, and recommendation checkpoints trained using the released SESRec and UniSAR implementations. Across three independently trained UniSAR checkpoints, the estimated all-source benefit depends on the control. On the same 66,139 rows, replacing all search inputs with a neutral ID yields a positive signed contribution, whereas replacing them with category/profile-matched observed search sequences gives smaller estimates, with an interval below zero for one checkpoint. The paired RR gaps range from $+2.770 \times 10^{-3}$ to $+6.604 \times 10^{-3}$, and every adjusted interval is above zero. Neutral masks change 59.7-61.7% of target ranks, while matched replacements change 44.1-44.8%. The control contrast persists across five alternative donor assignments per checkpoint. Under the primary neutral-mask and category-matched controls, positive latest-slot contribution is not established in SESRec or UniSAR. These results show why masking evidence should be compared with observed-search replacements when attributing a benefit to broader search state or the latest episode.
papers.summary: Worse recommendations after removing search history do not establish that its content provided the gain. FocalSwap fixes pre-search recommendation history, candidates and the model, then compares masking all search inputs with replacing them using real searches matched by category and behavioural profile. On 66139 shared UniSAR examples, masking supported a positive contribution from the original search state; matched replacements did not. Primary tests changing only the latest search also established no positive contribution. Attribution depends on the reference input, making observed-search replacement a useful check alongside masking ablations in search-augmented recommendation.

papers.title: Safe and Efficient Multi-Epoch Embedding Training
papers.abstract:
Authors: Shruthi Hariharan | Machine Learning Engineer II; Konish Dutta | Machine Learning Engineer II; Abhinav Naikawadi | Sr. Machine Learning Engineer; Zhihua Zhang | Machine Learning Engineer II; Rakshita Nagalla | Sr. Machine Learning Engineer; Kousik Rajesh* | Machine Learning Engineer II; Matt Lawhon | Staff Machine Learning Engineer
Tags: Machine Learning, Infrastructure, Recommendation Systems
Content Track: Technical Discussion / Architecture of big components

* == work done while at Pinterest

Introduction

Large ID embedding tables underpin some of the largest modeling advances at Pinterest, including teacher-model scaling and cross-domain pretraining for ranking and retrieval. These tables are first pre-trained to learn broadly useful Pin representations and then fine-tuned as part of the downstream surface-specific ranking model. Here, we’ll focus on the Homefeed ranking model.

The str
papers.summary: Training longer on the same recommendation data can hurt because of the embedding table rather than the entire model. Extending Pinterest Homefeed training from one epoch to two reduced its offline save metric by nearly 6%; freezing ID embeddings eliminated the regression. The team then trained the surrounding network first and enabled embedding adaptation later. Combined with systems changes such as overlapping lookup communication and computation, production deployment improved online saves by 1.09%. Embedding tables and other network components converge at different rates, so they need not share a single update schedule.

papers.title: Alternatives to Shallow Autoencoders for Collaborative Filtering
papers.authors: Mario Mallea, Angela Nebot, Francisco Mugica
papers.abstract: Collaborative filtering (CF) is a cornerstone of recommender systems and plays a relevant role in many modern applications. CF uses user-item interaction data to discover future preferences. Although deep learning models have shown promise in CF, Embarrassingly Shallow Autoencoders for Sparse Data (EASE) has gained attention for its outstanding ranking accuracy provided by its closed-form solution. EASE relies primarily on relationships among items to fit a full-rank high-dimensional linear mapping. We hypothesize that this design limits its capacity to capture similar but not equivalent fine-grained user relationships, consequently limiting its recommendation accuracy. This paper introduces an alternative formulation based on EASE that takes advantage of user-user information. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid model that combines both user-user and item-item adjacency distributions. Our experiments reveal that the proposed models outperform EASE on well-known recommendation benchmarks, highlighting the significance of including the user alternative in shallow autoencoder studies for CF.
papers.summary: The same user–item interaction table can yield different recommendations when solved through item or user relationships. This paper replaces EASE’s item-to-item linear weights with user-to-user weights and provides a hybrid closed-form solution: mix interaction records using user-to-user weights, then score candidates using item-to-item weights. On MovieLens, the hybrid raises NDCG@100 from EASE’s 40.95 to 43.51; on Gowalla, both new variants perform worse. Gains depend on relationship structure, while a user-to-user matrix also makes memory and inversion costs scale with the user population.

papers.title: OptST: Optimizing Semantic Tokenization for LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
papers.authors: Hanchong Chen, Jie Liu, Fuyuan Lyu, Dugang Liu, Lingjie Li, Xiuqiang He, Xing Tang
papers.abstract: Semantic information can enrich the identifiers and structured fields used by recommender systems. Semantic tokenization provides a structured representation of this information by converting LLM-derived user profiles into discrete tokens. In the common two-stage pipeline, the tokenizer is trained before the recommender. Its token assignments are then treated as fixed input features during recommendation training. As a result, the downstream recommender can learn how to use the assigned indices, but it cannot revise the semantic partition that produced them. Making this partition task-aware is difficult because nearest-code assignment is discrete, and unconstrained adaptation may also distort the geometry learned during pretraining. Moreover, a fixed token depth exposes the same semantic resolution to every interaction. We thus propose OptST (Optimizing Semantic Tokenization), which makes a pretrained tokenizer responsive to downstream recommendation. To revise token assignments without directly updating the pretrained encoder or base codebooks, OptST learns a low-rank deformation whose drift is limited by an anchor regularizer. Recommendation supervision reaches this transformation through a straight-through estimator, while prediction retains hard nearest-code assignments. Beyond adapting the assignments themselves, OptST selects an interaction-conditioned prefix to control how much residual detail is exposed to the recommender. Experiments on four public datasets show that OptST achieves the highest AUC among conventional and LLM-enhanced baselines. Its improvements also persist across different recommendation backbones. These results establish task-aware semantic tokenization as an effective interface between LLM-derived profiles and downstream recommendation models.
papers.summary: A frozen tokenizer can assign two users’ profiles the same token sequence, leaving the recommender unable to distinguish them through those tokens alone. At each step, reference vectors represent groups: the nearest vector to the remaining profile information supplies its token, and the unrepresented remainder is encoded next. OptST freezes the original encoder and reference vectors, learning a low-rank correction matrix for each step. Multiplying each reference vector by that matrix and adding the result to the original vector yields the effective assignment position; recommendation losses train the matrix. On Games offline, the complete system raised AUC from the frozen-tokenizer variant’s 0.7469 to 0.7532.

papers.title: PEARL: Prediction Error-Adaptive Regularized Learning for Selective Forgetting under Partial Preference Drift
papers.abstract: User preferences shift as needs, context, and tastes evolve. This matters for personalized recommendation, LLM response generation, and RLHF-trained reward models, which can become miscalibrated as preferences drift. Existing non-stationary bandit methods forget uniformly across all dimensions, but real preference shifts are typically partial: some dimensions go stale while others remain valid. Neural contextual bandits accumulate confidence monotonically via the Gram matrix, with no mechanism to direct uncertainty where predictions have gone wrong. We propose PEARL (Prediction Error-Adaptive Regularized Learning), which reverses the Gram update along feature directions where predictions are surprisingly wrong, while leaving confidence intact elsewhere. We prove that (i) any non-adaptive policy suffers linear regret after a preference shift, (ii) no fixed exploration rate achieves low regret in both stationary and non-stationary regimes, and (iii) PEARL's cumulative regret scales with the number of shifted users N_s, not the total population N. On PRISM, a personalized LLM response selection benchmark (1,500 users, 21 LLMs), PEARL beats greedy by +4.0 points and the best neural bandit baseline by +2.5 points (p<0.001), while performing on par with greedy when preferences are stable. It beats sliding-window and discounted approaches by 3 to 10 points, showing that selective forgetting outperforms uniform forgetting. The selection policy is a ~100K-parameter MLP that runs in milliseconds on CPU, leaves LLM weights frozen, and works with any API-based model.
papers.summary: After preferences change, updating a scoring model with new feedback alone may be slow to find better responses. PEARL uses a small selector for LLM responses: besides predicted ratings, candidates receive an uncertainty-based exploration bonus, weighted more heavily when a user’s recent observed ratings differ more from predictions. After PRISM tests artificially turned half the users’ high response ratings into low ratings and their low ratings into high ratings, mean reward at epoch 10 exceeded an equally online-updated model choosing only the highest predicted rating by 0.040. LLM weights stayed fixed. This supports active exploration under controlled drift, not online evidence of naturally changing preferences.

papers.title: One Basket, Many Experts: Decorrelated Re-ranking for Financial Asset Recommendation
papers.authors: Ryuki Unno, Keigo Sakurai, Koshi Watanabe, Keisuke Maeda, Takahiro Ogawa, Miki Haseyama
papers.abstract: Financial asset recommendation for retail investors is typically optimized for relevance, that is, how well a recommendation matches what each user will buy. From the service provider's point of view, the value of a recommendation also depends on portfolio performance: the risk-adjusted return the recommended assets (the basket) deliver, which drives user engagement and fee revenue. The two goals are rarely achieved jointly, because the recommendations that best match user behavior concentrate on a few popular assets whose returns are highly correlated, which caps the risk-adjusted return a provider can offer. We propose Decorrelated-Satellite Expert Re-ranking (\textbf{DSER}), which retains the most relevant recommendations from an expert-following list and replaces the rest with return-decorrelated alternatives. The number of replaced slots is a single integer~$m$ (a knob) that the provider sets, so the relevance--performance trade-off becomes an explicit, auditable choice rather than a property hidden inside a learned model. In experiments on the public FAR-Trans retail-brokerage dataset, under the primary protocol, replacing a few slots improves risk-adjusted return at a small relevance cost, and the gain survives realistic trading costs at typical retail portfolio sizes. Minimizing correlation would lower basket volatility, but in our data the least-correlated assets are more volatile and higher-return, so their volatility offsets that reduction while their return drives the gain, not lower volatility. The resulting trade-off is asymmetric, with the relevance cost consistent across market phases while the gain is phase-dependent. The provider sets $m$ to read off exactly how much relevance each operating point costs.
papers.summary: Asset recommendation must consider more than what users will buy: popular assets can move together. DSER first identifies investors with strong historical returns, ranking assets by their purchase counts weighted by returns. It preserves the ranking’s front and replaces trailing entries sequentially with the asset having the lowest return correlation to the current basket. The provider specifies the replacement count; no model training is required. In the main FAR-Trans experiment, benefits primarily came from higher-return replacements rather than lower basket volatility. With four replacements over six non-overlapping half-year windows, Sharpe improved only four times, while relevance to users’ actual purchases fell every time. Benefits depended on market phase; relevance costs were more stable.

papers.title: Tasteply: Externalizing Stable and Situational Preference as Manipulable Spatial Objects
papers.abstract: Most recommender systems treat user preferences as a single signal to infer and optimize, yet human preferences are a mix of a stable preference and situational preferences that turn on and off depending on context. Through Tasteply, we externalize this preference structure as manipulable spatial objects. Tasteply represents each situational preference as an attractor and the stable preference as an underlying global field. Users can adjust their feed by moving around the space and adjusting the strength of the global field, turning the preference structure that remains latent within the model into something they can see and act on directly to steer the recommendation algorithm. Through an exploratory study (N=5), we found that this spatial control was effective, along with its limits and future direction as a means of manipulating preference-based recommendations.
papers.summary: What users usually like and what they want in the current session need not coincide. Tasteply lets users organise liked posts by purpose, representing each group as a point on a map. Moving closer gives that group more influence on recommendations, while a separate slider adjusts the remaining stable preference signal. In an exploratory study with 5 researchers, this mixing suited casual exploration better; some preferred fixing one group when seeking specific information. The interface demonstrates how to expose preference controls, not evidence that recommendation quality has improved.
